body:
Howdy Scott,

I need some more details...

scorey@saber.net wrote in article <36053389.49CE@mail.saber.net>
(http://www.dejanews.com/getdoc.xp?AN=393123538):

>         This analysis makes me uncomfortable.  ISAIF demonstrates use
> of Ellul and frustration-aggression theory as "fixed ideas," if not
> obesessions, but other theoretical insights and concepts are handled
> with what I would call "casual mastery" of that literature.  Some of
> the latter were published long after TK is supposed to have closed his
> mental universe.

"Some of the latter" Such as?

Isn't it possible that these items were part of his framework long
before ISAIF?  I mean, there's plenty of his writing we haven't seen.

> Also, ISAIF is willing to entertain theoretical
> conflicts and uncertainty.  No future predictions or utopias are
> allowed, yet a "positive goal" is accepted as a practical necessity.
> An actual contradiction is introduced when the future of modern
> society (absent a revolution) is predicted in broad outline.
> Furthermore, leftists are judged bad because they are true believers,
> yet the anti-technology revolution will need true believers, too.
> Other people might have no problem with entertaining these conceptual
> tensions, but is it consistent with Johnson's analysis of TK?

Isn't it possible that, given time, TK can come up with a "positive
goal" to put down on paper.  And if so, isn't it possible that *on a
personal level* he doesn't have strong feelings about this positive
goal, and when dicsussing the issues verbally (not one of his strong
suits) that he can't come up with one?  ISAIF Paragraph 183 seems to
back this up.

     183. But an ideology, in order to gain enthusiastic support,
     must have a positive ideal as well as a negative one...

I forget the details of the '71 essay, but was this a problem TK saw
with it years later?  NO POSITIVE IDEAL and therefore, NO SUPPORT?
The recognition that anger and revenge don't really do it for anyone
but him?

There's plenty of evidence that TK doesn't care particularly about
wild nature. (The littering, the lack of mention in the 71 article,
and the weak mention in ISAIF.)  Probably just appreciates there not being
people around.  If one existed, an empty city or suburb would have done just
fine, too.  If he had money for it, he probably would have bought his carrots.

> 1) What is the supposed place of ISAIF in the life and mind of Ted
> Kaczynski?  How can its contents be explained in light of his
> diagnosis?  Just how "rough" is the rough draft found in the cabin?
> If positive goals are so insignificant, and avoidance of socially
> inflicted penalties so important to him, why did he take the chance on
> publication?

It seems TK struggled to understand his anger and need for revenge and it
probably helped to see himself as fighting for a cause.  Also, as
a writer (which TK probably considered himself), it's frustrating
for people not to read or respond what you've done.  His lack of
success with the 1971 essay?

> 2) Why did the prosecution not release journal entries describing his
> writing and sending of the letters and ISAIF, the way it released
> entries about his development of bombs?  Why did they argue in court
> that the cabin writings were honest and accurate self-confessions
> because they were never meant to be read by anyone else, even though
> several quotations that were released show how clearly Kaczynski
> anticipated the day when his writings would be discovered (planning
> that some would be destroyed as "bad public relations") and wrote some
> items (the whole autobiography, for instance) explicitly for a future
> audience.

Could you tell me when this happened?  I'd like to read the transcript.

> 6) If Theodore Kaczynski's memory is so strong that he can recite from
> his journals on demand, why are some of the journal entries about the
> bombings (which, one would suppose, were peak experiences of his life)
> uncertain about details of the events?  Why are some of the details
> probably false (Bomb #6 was sent in a different month, and probably with
> a different target than reported in the journals)?

Could you provide references?  Isn't some of this likely selective
memory?  Also, TK doesn't operate well in face-to-face so it's not
surprising that he would recite on autopilot.  I know some people
similar to this.

> 7) Is there any pattern in the cabin writings that would explain why
> they sometimes speak only of "I" while at other times they speak of
> "we"?

Accident?  What are some references to "we" besides those in ISAIF?

I need some references, references, references!

E
